# Fermentation is the work of living yeast (`fermentation_yeast`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/biology.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Life sciences (`biology`)
- Deps: helped by microscope, microorganisms, spontaneous_generation_refuted, thermometer_temperature
- Core idea: The scum and sediment in fermenting wine and beer contains living yeast, a fungus whose round cells bud and multiply. Even without oxygen, yeast turns sugar into alcohol and the gas that makes the froth; alcohol tolerance varies with the yeast and conditions. Wine turns to vinegar, beer goes ropy and milk sours because other, smaller organisms get in, each making its own product; the vinegar organism needs air. So brewers and vintners should scald their vessels, start each batch with yeast from a good one, let fermenting vessels vent gas and keep finished wine protected from air, and can stop spoilage by heating the finished drink in closed vessels to about 60 °C for some minutes, which kills the spoilers without cooking the wine.
- Pitfalls:
  - Calling yeast a chemical or dead sediment; Liebig, the leading chemist of 1840, said exactly that and mocked the microscopists
  - Boiling wine to preserve it, which ruins it; gentle heat is enough
  - Confusing fermentation with distillation; yeast alone cannot make spirits
  - Saying Pasteur was simply right: in 1897 Buchner showed that juice pressed from dead yeast still ferments sugar, so Liebig had part of the truth
- History: mesopotamia: c. 3500–3000 BC – beer residues at Godin Tepe; c. 1800 BC Hymn to Ninkasi describes brewing; egypt: c. 3000 BC onward – large-scale bread and beer making; china: c. 7000 BC – fermented rice, honey and fruit drink at Jiahu; mould starters (qu) for grain wine by the Han period; 12th c. texts describe heating wine to keep it; east_asia: 16th c. – Japanese brewers heat sake to preserve it, three centuries before Pasteur; europe: 1680 – Leeuwenhoek sees yeast globules; 1837–1838 Cagniard-Latour, Schwann and Kützing independently show yeast is alive; 1857–1860 Pasteur on lactic and alcoholic fermentation; 1866 heating of wine; 1883 Hansen's pure yeast cultures at Carlsberg; 1897 Buchner's cell-free fermentation
- Read:
  - Louis Pasteur, Mémoire sur la fermentation alcoolique (1860)
  - James A. Barnett, A history of research on yeasts 2: Louis Pasteur and his contemporaries, 1850–1880, Yeast (2000)
  - Patrick E. McGovern, Uncorking the Past: The Quest for Wine, Beer, and Other Alcoholic Beverages (2009)
